name: Fitzwilliam Museum
label: Fitzwilliam Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trumpington Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Trumpington Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/5649709: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fitzwilliam Museum' (167 m across).
notes: Grand neoclassical museum on Trumpington Street.

text.description:
The Fitzwilliam Museum is the art and antiquities museum of the University of Cambridge, and its front is a formal, symmetrical classical facade. A tall classical portico with columns and a carved pediment sits above a broad flight of stone steps. It is a formal, symmetrical building, so it suits a simple straight-on photo.

The museum was founded in 1816 under the will of Richard FitzWilliam, 7th Viscount FitzWilliam. The main building, called the Founder's Building, was put up between 1837 and 1843 to designs by George Basevi, and C. R. Cockerell completed it. The carving, including the four lions, is by William Grinsell Nicholl. The museum opened in 1848, and the building and its street-front boundary are Grade I listed.

For your photo, cross Trumpington Street and stand on the far pavement opposite the main entrance. From there you can take in the whole portico and the entrance in one frame. Keep the phone level so the columns stay upright, and leave a little space around the building rather than cropping tight. If you want a people photo, the steps below the columns make a neat formal backdrop. Round the back, Coe Fen gives a quieter view of the rear of the museum. Check that angle on the ground, as it is less well known.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in central Cambridge on Trumpington Street, opposite Fitzwilliam Street.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Trumpington Street in central Cambridge, where the museum stands opposite Fitzwilliam Street. From there the museum is just to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural, front-on view of the portico. If the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole building in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the columns, pediment and lions.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Trumpington Street (opposite the main entrance, across the road). The neoclassical portico and main entrance of the museum, framed straight on from the far pavement. From here you see the portico and main entrance straight on, and the museum lies just to the south-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the centre of the portico up with the middle of the frame, keeping the columns vertical. Leave some space above the pediment and some pavement or railings at the bottom. For a more formal people photo, try the museum steps instead, with the columns rising behind. Coe Fen gives a quieter view of the rear of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the portico keeps its detail. If the ultra-wide makes the edges lean, step back and use the default lens (1x) instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Even, soft daylight, such as a bright overcast day or the morning, tends to suit the pale stone. Earlier in the day there are usually fewer people on the steps.

text.access_note: The building can be photographed from the public pavement, and the museum is free to enter, with photography allowed inside without flash. It has been under restoration at times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The portico is a symmetrical, columned front that suits a straight-on photograph.
Even, soft daylight such as bright overcast or morning light tends to suit pale stone buildings.
There are usually fewer people on the steps earlier in the day.
The pavement opposite the entrance may be narrow, so the ultra-wide lens may help to fit the whole building in.

name: Market Hill
label: Market Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Great St Mary's' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'St Mary's Street' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8117433: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Market Square' (90 m across).
notes: Historic market square in the town centre.

text.description:
Market Hill, also called the Market Square, is the open marketplace in the middle of Cambridge. Trading has gone on here since Saxon times, and a daily outdoor market with stalls still runs today. That is the appeal for a photo: rows of stalls with coloured awnings, set against old college and church buildings. Great St Mary's, the University Church, stands on the west side. Its tower looks over King's Parade. The Guildhall, built in the 1930s, is on the south side.

The square was mostly filled with buildings until a major fire in 1849 led to it being cleared. In 1855 a Gothic Revival fountain went up in the middle, and most of it was pulled down in 1953. It once had a water supply from Hobson's Conduit, finished in 1614.

From there you look straight down on the stalls and their awnings, with King's College Chapel and the college rooftops beyond. It is about 123 steps to the top. If you would rather stay at street level, the square itself gives a ground-level view of the stalls, with the stone tower rising behind them. On busy market days, stalls and vans can block that view, so move around until you find a gap. Check the official site before you go up the tower.
text.geographic_location: Market Hill is the central market square of Cambridge, just east of King's Parade. Great St Mary's church stands on its west side and the Guildhall on its south side.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stops are listed nearby, so head for King's Parade in the centre of Cambridge. Great St Mary's, with its tower, stands on King's Parade and on the west side of Market Hill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start on the default lens (1x) to take in the whole square from above. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the awnings or King's College Chapel in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Great St Mary's (climb the tower; look down over the square). A bird's-eye view of the market square below, with rows of stalls and their colourful awnings, with King's College Chapel and the college rooftops beyond. For the ground-level alternative, walk about 1 minute east into Market Hill itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From the tower, use the gridlines to line up the rows of stalls and leave the chapel and rooftops in the upper third of the picture. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full spread, then zoom in for a tighter picture of the awnings. As an alternative, shoot from the square with the stalls in the foreground and the stone tower of Great St Mary's rising behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the awnings to set focus, then use the exposure slider to stop bright sky washing out the rooftops. Hold the phone steady against your body, and keep a firm grip on it when leaning out over any edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a day and time when the stalls are up, since the awnings are the point of the view from above. Check the official site for tower opening times before you go. The Guildhall side of the square is usually in shade, so expect more even light on the other sides.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but the tower is a paid, ticketed climb, so check the official site before you go for prices and opening times.
claims_not_in_sources: Stalls and vans can block the ground-level view when the market is busy.
The Guildhall side of the square is usually in shade.
Great St Mary's tower is a paid climb with about 123 steps; tickets and opening times should be checked on the official site.
The awnings are best seen when the stalls are set up, during market hours.
King's College Chapel and the college rooftops can be seen beyond the square from the top of the tower.

name: Mathematical Bridge
label: Mathematical Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Silver Street Bridge' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Silver Street' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/570076432: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Mathematical Bridge' (17 m across).
notes: Wooden footbridge at Queens' College.

text.description: The Mathematical Bridge is a small wooden footbridge across the River Cam that links two parts of Queens' College. It looks like a smooth arch, but it is built entirely from straight timbers, laid as a series of tangents and tied together with cross-pieces. That is where the name comes from, and it is why the bridge looks so neat in a photo: the criss-cross of timber shows up well against the water and the college buildings behind. The design is by William Etheridge, and James Essex built it in 1749. It has been rebuilt twice, in 1866 and 1905, but keeps the same shape, and it is Grade II listed. You may hear that Isaac Newton built it without bolts. He died over twenty years before it was built, so that story is a myth. The best-known photo is a side view from the footpath on Silver Street Bridge, looking upstream, with the wooden span in the middle and Queens' College behind. It is free to reach on foot, but it can get busy with other people taking the same picture, so be patient and take your turn at the rail. Keep your phone steady against the parapet, take a few frames, and wait for a gap if a punt drifts through. The bridge itself is not a free public crossing, so this view from the street is the easy way to see it.
text.geographic_location: In the southwest of central Cambridge, on the River Cam between two parts of Queens' College, about a stone's throw northwest of Silver Street Bridge.
text.directions_text: There are no nearby stations or tram stops, so head for Silver Street and Queens' College in the southwest of central Cambridge and walk to Silver Street Bridge. Stand on its public footpath. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic side view of the whole bridge with the college behind it. If other people are in the way, switch to telephoto (2x or 3x) to pick out just the timber arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Silver Street Bridge (public footpath on the bridge, looking upstream toward the Mathematical Bridge). A wide classic view of the wooden bridge over the River Cam with Queens' College buildings behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge up along one of the horizontal lines so the arch looks level. Leave a little water in the bottom of the frame. For a different angle, try Silver Street, at the street end, where boats passing through the scene add interest.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the timbers to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the wood keeps its colour. Take a short burst or a Live Photo while a punt passes, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people.

text.access_note: The view from Silver Street Bridge is from a public footpath, but the Mathematical Bridge itself is for Queens' College members and paying visitors only, so check the official site before you go if you want to visit the college.
claims_not_in_sources: Calm water can give a reflection of the bridge in the lower part of the frame.
Dropping the exposure slider slightly helps in bright sky and keeps the wood's colour.
You can steady the phone against the parapet of Silver Street Bridge.

name: The Eagle
label: The Eagle pub
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bene't Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bene't Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/149032866: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Eagle' (42 m across).
notes: Pub where the discovery of DNA's structure was announced.

text.description:
The Eagle is a Grade II listed pub in the middle of Cambridge, and it is a pleasing subject for a quick phone photo. The front, on the north side of Bene't Street, dates from around 1600. It is a cream stone façade with a central entrance, and the narrow street gives it a tidy, framed look. The pub opened in 1667 as a coaching inn and is the second oldest pub in the city. Behind the front is a galleried 19th-century wing facing a courtyard.

The Eagle is also known for science. On 28 February 1953 Francis Crick announced here that he and James Watson had 'discovered the secret of life', their proposed structure of DNA. A blue plaque next to the entrance commemorates this, so it is worth catching in your picture. In the Second World War, Allied airmen wrote their names and squadron numbers on the ceiling of the rear bar.

For the standard exterior shot, stand on the opposite side of Bene't Street and photograph the whole front, with the entrance in the middle. Keep the phone level so the walls stay upright, and let the street lead the eye towards the door. If you are allowed into the courtyard, the arched entrance, cobbles and timber gallery make a second, more intimate picture. The courtyard is inside the pub, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Eagle is at 8 Bene't Street in the centre of Cambridge, on the north side of the street. It is close to Corpus Christi College, which owns the site, and to Free School Lane.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for the centre of Cambridge and look for Bene't Street in the city centre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole three-storey front. If you cannot step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep the phone level so the building does not lean. For details such as the blue plaque or the signage, use telephoto (2x-3x).
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bene't Street (opposite the pub, facing west-southwest toward the front façade). The full three-storey cream stone front of The Eagle with its central entrance, framed along the narrow street. From there the pub front is to the north-west, across the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the central entrance up with the middle vertical line, with the three storeys filling the frame. Wait for a gap in passing people if you can, or include one or two for scale. If you can get into the courtyard, photograph the arched entrance and the timber gallery above it as a second picture; this is the alternative view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky or the pale stone looks washed out. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest view of the façade.

text.access_note: The front of the pub can be photographed from the public street, but the courtyard is inside the pub's grounds, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Because the pub is on the north side of Bene't Street, its front faces roughly south and tends to get sunlight during the middle of the day.
Pedestrians and cyclists often pass along the street while you are taking photographs.
Gridlines and a level phone help to keep the vertical lines of a building straight.

name: Kettle's Yard
label: Kettle's Yard
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'St Peter's churchyard' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'St Peter's Street' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/146626435: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kettle's Yard' (38 m across).
notes: Art gallery and house museum.

text.description:
Kettle's Yard is an art gallery and house on the west side of Castle Street, in the stretch between Northampton Street and St Peter's Church. It began as four small cottages, which Jim and Helen Ede converted into one unusual home after moving to Cambridge in 1956. Jim Ede gave the house and his collection of early 20th-century art to the University of Cambridge in 1966. Both the house and the gallery reopened in February 2018 after a building project that added new entrance and courtyard areas, so the frontage is newer than many older photos show.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the contrast between the old cottage front and the plainer modern additions. The best quiet view is from St Peter's churchyard, where you can look across at the cottage front of the house with the church close by in the frame. This is a calmer alternative to the street. If you want the street-facing brick and glazed facade shot straight on, use the pavement on Castle Street instead.

Keep the shot simple. Include a little of the churchyard in the foreground to give depth, and keep the vertical lines of the cottages upright by holding your phone level. The house is a working gallery, so be considerate of visitors and staff. Check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside or want to take photos indoors.
text.geographic_location: Kettle's Yard is on the west side of Castle Street in central Cambridge, between Northampton Street and St Peter's Church.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head to Castle Street in central Cambridge, between Northampton Street and St Peter's Church. Kettle's Yard is on the west side of the street, next to St Peter's Church. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the cottage front. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to include more of the churchyard and the church, and keep the phone level to avoid leaning walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in St Peter's churchyard (churchyard beside St Peter's Church, looking across at the Kettle's Yard house). The old cottage front of Kettle's Yard House seen across the churchyard, with the church nearby in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the gridlines to keep the walls and windows straight, and place the house on one third of the frame with the church or churchyard filling the rest. For a straight-on view of the brick and glazed facade, walk round to the Castle Street pavement as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest wall to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky and white window frames don't wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a bright but softly overcast day, or go earlier or later in the day when the light on the walls is gentler and the street is quieter.

text.access_note: Castle Street is a public road, but the churchyard view depends on the churchyard being open, and the gallery and house may have ticketed or timed entry, so check the official site before you go.

name: Corpus Clock
label: Corpus Clock
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trumpington Street' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/298290448: the OpenStreetMap point 'Corpus Clock'.
notes: Golden clock topped with the Chronophage.

text.description:
The Corpus Clock is a large gold-faced sculptural clock set into the outside wall of the Taylor Library at Corpus Christi College, on the corner of Bene't Street and Trumpington Street, looking out over King's Parade. The face is a rippling disc of gold-plated stainless steel, about 1.5 metres across. It has no hands or numbers. Instead, slits open in three rings, lit from behind with blue LEDs, to show the hours, minutes and seconds. On top sits a metal, grasshopper-like creature called the Chronophage, or 'time eater'. It moves its mouth as if eating the seconds and now and then blinks. The clock was unveiled in 2008 and sits in what used to be the entrance to a Victorian bank branch.

It photographs well because it has three things in one frame: the glowing blue and gold face, the odd, slightly menacing creature, and the old stonework around it. The face is glossy, so reflections can spoil a shot. The corner is narrow and the traffic is constant, so avoid standing close. Take your photos from across the road, where you can fit the whole clock in and stay clear of the pavement and the traffic. Stay on the pavement even if others step into the road.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Cambridge, on the corner of Trumpington Street and Bene't Street, on the outside of Corpus Christi College's Taylor Library and facing King's Parade.
text.directions_text: The clock is in central Cambridge, at the junction of Bene't Street and Trumpington Street, looking over King's Parade. The map marker is at the clock itself. For the best shot, cross to the opposite side of Trumpington Street, taking care with the traffic. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from across the road to take in the whole clock and some of the corner. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the gold face and the grasshopper. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the street scene around the clock, as it makes the clock look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The map marker sits at the clock itself, but the recommended viewpoint is across Trumpington Street, on the corner opposite. From there the gold face, the blue time display and the grasshopper on top all fit in the frame against the street corner. If you want a little more room, Bene't Street is reported to give a bit more space.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the centre of the face near the middle of the frame, with the grasshopper just above it. Stay square-on if you can, as the glossy face can reflect buildings, cars and you. If you see a reflection, take a step to one side and try again. A Live Photo or a short video will catch the creature's mouth moving and its blink.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gold face to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the blue LEDs stay crisp and don't wash out. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the blue LEDs are lit and traffic is lighter. Early morning is also suggested if you want fewer people around.

text.access_note: The clock is on the outside of the college library at street level, but you cannot go into the college to get closer; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Standing on the pavement across Trumpington Street is a safe place to photograph the clock from.
A Live Photo or short video on a phone can capture the creature's mouth movement and blinking.
Bracing your elbows against your body helps keep a phone steady in night mode.
The clock sits in the historic city centre of Cambridge.

name: Wren Library
label: Wren Library
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trinity Bridge' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Trinity Bridge' (way/166155996): middle (20 m across); moved 15 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9449788: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Wren Library' (66 m across).
notes: Christopher Wren's library at Trinity College.

text.description: The Wren Library is the library of Trinity College, designed by Christopher Wren in 1676 and completed in 1695. It is a single large room built over an open colonnade on the ground floor of Nevile's Court. From the river side it looks calm and plain. That simplicity is why it photographs well: a long, balanced building with the River Cam in front gives you a tidy, symmetrical picture with water, stone and sky. The library was one of the first to have large windows so readers could work in comfortable light, and you can see the rhythm of those windows along the front. It is a Grade I listed building and holds rare books and manuscripts, including Isaac Newton's copy of the Principia and A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh manuscript. The best outside view is from Trinity Bridge, looking at the river-facing side of the library with the water in the foreground. If you want a second angle, the grassy bank of the Backs opposite shows the library across the Cam, often with punts and people on the water in front of it. Photography inside the library is not permitted, so make the exterior your picture. The library is open to the public, but only for limited hours, and college grounds can be restricted outside visiting times. Check Trinity College's official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Cambridge, in Trinity College, whose river side looks onto the River Cam along the Backs. The library is built over the ground floor of Nevile's Court.
text.directions_text: Head for the Backs, the riverside area behind Trinity College in central Cambridge, reached on foot from the city centre. Check Trinity College's opening times first, as access to the grounds can be restricted. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole river-facing side of the library fits with the water in front. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want more of the river and sky. Move to 2x if you want to fill the frame with the long line of windows and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Trinity Bridge. The river-facing side of the Wren Library, with its plain façade and the Cam in the foreground, seen from the bridge. From there the library's river-facing side is to the north-east, with the Cam running in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the base of the building up with a horizontal line so the plain façade sits level. Keep a strip of river in the foreground. For a different view, try the grassy bank of the Backs opposite the library, where punts often drift across the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the library's stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the façade keeps its detail. If the river is still, a Live Photo can catch passing punts.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people on the bridge, and soft light from an overcast sky or the low sun shows the stonework well.

text.access_note: The library is open to the public with limited opening times and photography inside is not permitted; access to college grounds can be restricted, so check Trinity College's official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning usually means fewer people on Trinity Bridge.
Soft light from an overcast sky or low sun shows stonework well.
Setting gridlines level with the base of the building helps keep the façade straight in a phone photo.

name: Clare College
label: Clare College
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Clare Bridge' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Clare Bridge' (way/570077176): middle (24 m across); moved 15 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/139308034: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Clare College (University of Cambridge)' (300 m across).
notes: Elegant court and Clare Bridge on the Cam.

text.description:
Clare is one of Cambridge's oldest colleges, and its river side is the part most visitors photograph. The college began in 1326 as University Hall and is the second-oldest surviving college in the university, after Peterhouse. It was refounded as Clare Hall in 1338 with Elizabeth de Clare's endowment, and became Clare College in 1856. The Old Court, built between 1638 and 1715, is Grade I listed. You can see the style shift from late Gothic in the oldest wing to a fully classical look in the last block.

The best-known picture is taken from Clare Bridge, built in 1640 and the oldest of Cambridge's current bridges. It has fourteen stone balls, and one has a piece missing, which gives guides a good story to tell. From the middle of the bridge you can look back across the Cam at the college's river front. King's College Chapel rises behind the buildings, and the bridge's stone balls and arches frame the scene. Old Court is also known for framing the Chapel in views from the Backs.

Take a few frames in portrait and landscape, and keep the bridge's stonework in the foreground to give the picture depth. If the bridge is busy, wait for a gap rather than rushing. If you have time, try Garret Hostel Bridge or the Backs for a second angle on the same buildings.
text.geographic_location: Clare College is in central Cambridge, on the Backs beside the River Cam. Clare Bridge links its Old Court to Memorial Court on the far side of the river.
text.directions_text: Start from King's Parade in the centre of Cambridge, which leads to the college grounds where Clare Bridge stands. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of river front, bridge and Chapel. Switch to telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the roofline and the Chapel behind. The ultra-wide (0.5x) is useful only if you want the bridge's balls and arch very large in the foreground, and it can make the college look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Clare Bridge (middle of the bridge, looking back across the Cam at the college's river front). The college's river-facing buildings with King's College Chapel rising behind them, framed by the bridge's stone balls and arches. Turn to look back across the Cam at the college's river front, with the college just to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the Chapel up with the buildings so it sits behind them, not cut off by a corner. Let a stone ball or the curve of the parapet fill one lower corner as a frame. Keep the phone level so the college's vertical lines stay straight. For a different angle, Garret Hostel Bridge shows the college's buildings along the west bank, often with punts in front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework of the buildings to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady, or brace it on the parapet, for the sharpest result.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or soft low light, when there are fewer people and the light is gentler. Evening light is also worth trying from the Backs, where warm light falls on the college's west-facing walls.

text.access_note: Clare Bridge sits within college grounds, so follow the college's access rules and check the official site before you go; the Fellows' Garden is open to the public mainly over the summer months after exams in June.
claims_not_in_sources: Keeping the phone level helps keep vertical lines of buildings straight.
Dragging the exposure slider down helps keep detail in stonework when the sky is bright.
The bridge can be busy enough that you may need to wait for a gap to take a clear photo.
The ultra-wide lens can make distant buildings look smaller in the frame.

name: Cambridge University Botanic Garden
label: Botanic Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Main Lawn' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Main Lawn' (way/375944231): middle (135 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/3998385: large area 'Cambridge University Botanic Garden' (817 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: 40-acre garden with glasshouses and lake.

text.description:
Cambridge University Botanic Garden is a 16-hectare garden south of the city centre, laid out on flat ground with a lake, a rock garden and a long range of glasshouses. It was created for the University in 1831 by Professor John Stevens Henslow, Charles Darwin's teacher, and opened to the public in 1846. Today it holds more than 8,000 plant species from around the world. The lake was cleverly made from an old gravel pit, and the glasshouses date from the 1860s.

The classic view for a phone is on the Main Lawn. Face the glasshouses with the fountain in the foreground, and you get water, lawn and glass in a single frame, with the building rising neatly behind the fountain. If you want a second picture, the Lake gives calm reflections and lots of greenery, and the Glasshouse Range is best photographed from outside.

The garden is large and flat, so it is easy to wander and take your time. Personal photography is welcome, but drones are not allowed, and portrait, wedding or commercial shoots need advance permission. Commercial photography is not permitted inside the Glasshouse Range, so keep to outside views of the glass. Opening arrangements can change, and parts of the glasshouses have been closed at times, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the south of Cambridge, in the area bounded by Trumpington Road to the west, Bateman Street to the north and Hills Road to the east. The garden lies to the south of the town centre.
text.directions_text: No rail or tram stop is listed for this spot. The garden lies south of the centre of Cambridge, with entrances on Bateman Street, Hills Road and Trumpington Road (at the Brookside corner). Once inside, follow the paths to the Main Lawn and look for the fountain with the glasshouses behind it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the fountain and glasshouses together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lawn feels crowded or you want more sky and planting. Use 2x or more to pick out the glasshouse roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Main Lawn (stand on the lawn facing the glasshouses, with the fountain in the foreground). The fountain on the Main Lawn in the foreground with the glasshouses rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the fountain low in the frame and let the glasshouses rise behind it. Turn on the gridlines and keep the glass roofline level. If you want a different view, try the Lake for reflections, or the outside of the Glasshouse Range for the architecture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the glass or the fountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or the glass washes out. Take a few frames, as moving water looks different each time. Live Photos can catch the fountain spray.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when the light is soft, in the morning or later in the afternoon, and try for a quieter moment on the lawn. Check the official site first for current opening times.

text.access_note: A managed garden with several entrances; personal photography is allowed but drones are banned, so check the official site before you go.

name: Round Church
label: Round Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bridge Street' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Bridge Street and Round Church Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/92878394: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Round Church' (35 m across).
notes: Norman round church.

text.description: The Round Church, properly the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, is a small stone church with a conical roof, standing on the corner of Round Church Street and Bridge Street. It photographs well because its shape is so unlike the buildings around it, and the carved Norman west doorway gives you a strong detail to put in the frame. The church was built around 1130 and took its round shape from the rotunda of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. It began as a wayfarers' chapel beside the old Roman road that is now Bridge Street. It is one of only four medieval round churches still in use in England, and it has been Grade I listed since 1950. The best-known view is from the corner of the two streets, looking at the west front and the doorway, with the street edges giving a natural frame. The church is low and surrounded by taller buildings, so the light reaches it only at certain times of day. Bridge Street is busy with vans and cyclists, so wait for a gap before you shoot. The exterior is only really easy to see from the west and north sides. Inside there is an exhibition, but entry may be paid and photography may not be welcome, so this spot is about the outside view.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Cambridge, on the corner of Round Church Street and Bridge Street. The Cambridge Union Society's premises were built in the church's former graveyard.
text.directions_text: There is no railway or tram stop listed for this spot. The church can be reached on foot from the centre of Cambridge: head for the corner of Bridge Street and Round Church Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the church looks natural. If the pavement is too tight to fit the roof and doorway in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x or more) for the doorway carvings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Bridge Street and Round Church Street (corner facing the west front and Norman west door). The round stone church with its conical roof and the Norman west doorway, framed by the corner of the two streets.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and keep the walls upright by holding the phone level. Put the doorway on one of the lines and let the conical roof rise above it. If you want a different view, try St John's Street for the church seen down the street among the taller buildings, or Round Church Street for the church beside the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. If the front is in shadow, lift the exposure slightly. Wait for a gap in the traffic before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, before the sun drops behind St John's College. The front of the church is in shadow in the morning, so check your exposure.

text.access_note: The outside can be seen from the street, but the church is open to visitors as a managed site, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide (0.5x) lens helps when the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole church in the frame.
Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps keep the walls upright in the photo.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in the stonework when the sky is bright.

name: The Backs
label: The Backs
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Clare Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Clare Bridge' (way/570077176): middle (24 m across); moved 15 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/1999158: large area 'The Backs' (813 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Riverside meadows behind the colleges.

text.description: The Backs is the stretch of riverside lawns, trees and college grounds where several Cambridge colleges back on to the River Cam, with land on both banks. It photographs well because the elements stack up neatly: water in front, green lawns, old stone bridges and college buildings behind. From the lawns beside Clare Bridge you can look toward the pale Gothic front of King's College Chapel rising above the river, which is the classic view here. Clare Bridge is described by guides as one of the oldest and best-known bridges on the Backs. In 2013 National Trust chairman Simon Jenkins put the Backs in his top ten views in England, and since 1995 English Heritage has listed it as a Grade 1 Historic Park. It was once pasture, gardens and orchards, and cattle can still be seen grazing behind King's College. That gives you a nice chance of a foreground subject on the grass. For a phone shot, keep the river or a curve of the bridge in the lower part of the frame and let the chapel sit behind it. Go early if you can, as punts and tour groups fill the river later. If another bridge suits your walk better, Kitchen Bridge and the Bridge of Sighs, both near St John's College, offer different angles on the river and the stonework.
text.geographic_location: The Backs lies in central Cambridge, east of Queen's Road, where the college grounds meet the River Cam. Clare Bridge is the bridge spanning the Cam at Clare College, whose buildings are on the east bank; King's College is next along on the Backs.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Cambridge city centre, near the colleges, and head west toward the river and Queen's Road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full scene of river, lawn and chapel. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the bridge is crowded and you want more of the lawn and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring King's College Chapel closer without leaving the path.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Clare Bridge (from the Backs lawns beside the bridge, looking toward King's College Chapel). The classic view of King's College Chapel's pale Gothic façade rising behind the river, lawns and Clare College's buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the river along the lower third, with the chapel on one of the upper third lines. Keep the bridge's stone edge or a tree trunk at one side to give depth. Hold the phone steady and level, as the chapel's vertical lines show up quickly if you tilt. As an alternative, try Kitchen Bridge or the Bridge of Sighs for a different view of the stonework along the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the stone keep their detail. Try a Live Photo to catch movement on the water, such as a passing punt.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the punts and tour groups arrive, is the quietest time for this view.

text.access_note: The riverside paths are public, but some parts of the Backs are college grounds with limited access, so check the official site before you go.

name: Great St Mary's Church
label: Great St Mary's
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'King's Parade' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of King's Parade nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26344507: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Great Saint Mary, The University Church' (50 m across).
notes: University church with a tower viewing platform over the city.

text.description:
Great St Mary's is the University Church of Cambridge, standing at the north end of King's Parade opposite the Senate House. It is a Grade I listed building in the Late Perpendicular Gothic style. The present church was built between 1478 and 1519, and the tower was finished later, in 1608. The University Clock inside chimes the Cambridge Quarters, which were later borrowed for Big Ben. In 2018 the funeral of Stephen Hawking was held here.

It photographs well because the Gothic front and tower sit right on the street, so you can frame them with the buildings along King's Parade. King's College and its Chapel are visible further down the street, which gives the picture a sense of place.

Take a wide shot first to show the whole street, then move in for a tighter picture of the tower and the stonework. If Market Hill is nearby, it gives a different view of the church across the open square, with shopfronts and people in the foreground. Senate House Passage gives a narrower, framed view. These two are worth checking on the ground. Keep an eye on passing traffic, cyclists and pedestrians before you step back to line up a shot.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Cambridge, at the north end of King's Parade, across the street from the Senate House.
text.directions_text: Great St Mary's is at the north end of King's Parade in central Cambridge. If you are coming from further out, head to the city centre and then walk to King's Parade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street view of the church front and tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the whole tower in the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-3x, or up to 5x on some phones) for a tighter shot of the tower and carved stone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on King's Parade (north end, opposite the Senate House, facing south down the street). The church's Gothic front and tower framed along the street, with King's College and its Chapel visible further down the parade.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and let the street lead the eye towards the church, with the tower on one side of the frame. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean. If you want a different view, Market Hill shows the church across the open square, and Senate House Passage gives a narrower, framed view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its detail and the stone is not washed out. Wait for a gap in the passing people and bikes before you take the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually calmer on the street. Softer light on a bright day makes the stonework look better, but the view is worth taking at any time.

text.access_note: The church is an active place of worship and a university church, so please be respectful if you go inside, and check the official site before you go for visiting times and any tower access.
claims_not_in_sources: The view from King's Parade is usually quieter early in the morning.
Softer light shows stonework better than harsh midday sun.
King's Parade carries pedestrians, cyclists and some traffic that you may need to wait for.
The tower may need a separate ticket to climb, so check the official site before you go.

name: King's Parade
label: King's Parade
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Senate House Hill' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Senate House Hill nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/3993048: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'King's Parade' (146 m long).
notes: Historic street facing King's College.

text.description:
King's Parade is a street at the heart of university Cambridge. King's College runs along the west side, and the east end of its large Chapel closes the scene. Across the road is a row of mostly touristy shops, and Great St Mary's, the University Church, stands opposite the Senate House. The Senate House is mainly used for degree ceremonies, and this top end of the street is known as Senate House Hill. The college gatehouse and screen date from the 1830s, when the old west side of the street was cleared to make room for them. The Corpus Clock, added in 2008, sits at the southern end.

It photographs well because so much is packed into one view: stone, pinnacles, old shopfronts and a lively mix of cyclists and students in term-time. The best phone picture from Senate House Hill pairs the Chapel with the Senate House at the top of the parade, with the Senate House in the frame. It also keeps you a little away from the busiest spot at the gatehouse. Take your time over the composition and wait for a gap between cyclists. If you want the gatehouse in the foreground with the Chapel rising behind it, walk down the parade a short way for a second shot.
text.geographic_location: King's Parade is in central Cambridge, in the old university area, with King's College along its west side. The street continues north as Trinity Street and south as Trumpington Street.
text.directions_text: Head for central Cambridge and the University area and look for King's College or the Senate House. From there the middle of King's Parade is about 1 minute on foot to the south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the Chapel, the Senate House and the street together. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Chapel's pinnacles at the far end.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Senate House Hill (north end, near the Senate House, looking back toward the chapel). A view that pairs the Chapel with the Senate House at the top of the parade, with the Senate House in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the street up with a vertical grid line so the buildings stand straight. Let the street lead the eye towards the Chapel. For a different angle, Trinity Street gives a quieter view south along the approach to the parade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the buildings keep their detail. Try a Live Photo to catch cyclists passing, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early mornings are recommended because the parade is busy with visitors later in the day. The Chapel has also been photographed here in snow.

text.access_note: The street is open to the public, but photography is restricted inside King's College Chapel, and many college courts may require permission for commercial shoots, so check with the porters' lodges.

name: Bridge of Sighs
label: Bridge of Sighs
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kitchen Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kitchen Bridge' (way/570077179): middle (22 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/576816647: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bridge of Sighs' (20 m across).
notes: Covered bridge over the Cam at St John's College.

text.description:
The Bridge of Sighs is a stone covered bridge at St John's College. It carries the college across the River Cam, linking Third Court with New Court. It was designed by Henry Hutchinson in the Gothic Revival style and finished in 1831. It is Grade I listed. The name comes from the famous bridge in Venice, though the two have little in common beyond being covered and having arched bases. Queen Victoria is said to have loved it more than anywhere else in Cambridge, and it has appeared in The Theory of Everything and in a Pink Floyd video.

It photographs well because it is compact and decorative. The pale stonework, the arched base and the water below sit neatly in one frame. You can't walk onto the bridge without entering the college, so the best free view is from Kitchen Bridge, the neighbouring Wren-designed bridge. Stand on it and look across the river toward the covered bridge. The River Cam fills the foreground, and that view is often called the best on-foot view of the bridge. It works best in good weather. It can also get busy, so be patient and take your shot when people move out of the way. If you have time, The Backs, the lawns beside the river, offer a second view, often with willow branches framing the stonework.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is inside St John's College, in the central riverside part of Cambridge known as the Backs, where it crosses the River Cam between Third Court and New Court.
text.directions_text: Head for the Backs on the west side of the River Cam in central Cambridge. Make your way to Kitchen Bridge, the neighbouring bridge next to St John's College. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the bridge, the river and some of the buildings around it. Then try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the covered bridge. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of river and sky, and keep the bridge away from the edges of the frame, where it may look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kitchen Bridge (stand on the bridge and look across the river toward the covered bridge). The covered Bridge of Sighs framed from the neighbouring Wren-designed bridge, with the River Cam in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the Bridge of Sighs on one of the third lines, with the river filling the lower part of the picture. Keep the horizon level and the bridge's arch centred over its reflection if you can. For a different view, walk to The Backs and photograph the bridge across the river from the lawns, using willow branches to frame the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stonework to focus and set the exposure. If the sky is bright, slide the exposure down a little so the detail doesn't wash out. Wait for the water to settle before you shoot, or try a Live Photo and choose the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a day with good weather. Visit early or late in the day if you can, as the spot is popular and the crowds are likely to be smaller.

text.access_note: Kitchen Bridge is open to the public, but going into St John's College to walk the bridge or see its courts is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Kitchen Bridge and The Backs are busy, so expect crowds and waits.
Early or late in the day is likely to be quieter than the middle of the day.
Waiting for the water to settle can give a calmer reflection of the bridge.

name: Senate House
label: Senate House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'King's Parade' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of King's Parade nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/5094870: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Senate House' (39 m across).
notes: Neoclassical university ceremonial building.

text.description: The Senate House is a neoclassical building of the University of Cambridge, built in pale Portland stone to a design by James Gibbs. Building ran from 1722 to 1730, and the western end was only finished in 1768. It was meant to form one side of a quadrangle, but the rest was never built, so it stands as a single, elegant block. Today it is used mainly for graduation ceremonies, and it is Grade I listed. It photographs well because the front is symmetrical, with clean lines and a pale stone that stands out against the old colleges around it. Look for the balcony and the roofline. Students have a long record of pranks up there, including an Austin Seven van that appeared on the roof in 1958. The building is not open to the public, so you will be shooting from the street. Keep your phone level, use the gridlines to keep the columns upright, and take a few frames with different amounts of pavement and sky.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Cambridge, on King's Parade, between King's College and Gonville and Caius College. It forms part of the university's Old Schools Site, close to Great St Mary's church.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Cambridge and the stretch of King's Parade opposite the Senate House, near Great St Mary's. From there the Senate House is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the whole front without distortion. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) only if people or traffic force you to stand closer, and keep the building centred to avoid stretched edges. Use telephoto (2x or more) for the balcony, the pediment and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on King's Parade (opposite the Senate House, near Great St Mary's (Senate House Hill)). The full neoclassical front of the Senate House across the street, framed by the church opposite. From here the full neoclassical front is visible across the street, with Great St Mary's close by.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the columns up with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep the phone level and include a little pavement and sky. For a different view, try Senate House Passage, a narrow angle along the side of the building with Gonville & Caius College opposite, or Trinity Street for a longer view away from the King's Parade crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building's pale stone to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the stone does not wash out against the sky. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually the quietest, with fewer people in the frame. On a bright day, a little cloud helps keep the stone from glaring. Evening with night mode also works.

text.access_note: The Senate House is not open to the public, so you photograph it from the street; the lawn may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning on King's Parade is usually quieter, with fewer people in the frame.
Graduation days may bring crowds and some restrictions around the building.
Thin cloud softens glare on pale stone, and the stone can wash out on a bright day.
King's Parade is a public street open for photography.

name: Magdalene Bridge
label: Magdalene Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quayside' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Quayside' (way/128363757): middle (80 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/3992970: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Magdalene Street' (135 m long).
notes: Bridge with punts at the Quayside.

text.description: Magdalene Bridge is the cast-iron bridge that carries the street over the River Cam, just south of Magdalene College and just north of St John's College. The bridge you see today dates from 1823 and was designed by the Norwich architect Arthur Browne. It is a single span of iron, with a railing along the top that ends in stone piers. It has been Grade II listed since 1969. There has been a crossing here for a very long time: a series of wooden bridges stood on the spot from Anglo-Saxon times until James Essex built a stone one in 1754, and the original crossing is what gave Cambridge its name. It photographs well from the water's edge. The curve of the iron span sits over the river, with punts moored or drifting underneath and the riverside buildings along the quays on either side. From the Quayside you look back at the bridge across the water, so the river gives you a natural foreground and the bridge forms the centre of the picture. Punts can drift into the view, so wait a moment for a clear gap or use one as part of the shot. If you have time, the old buildings on Magdalene Street, some dating from the 16th century, are worth a walk and a few extra pictures. For a different angle, the opposite bank gives a side-on view of the bridge across the river.
text.geographic_location: In the north of central Cambridge, where Magdalene Street crosses the River Cam on the bridge and continues south-east as Bridge Street. It sits just south of Magdalene College and just north of St John's College.
text.directions_text: Head for the Quayside on the river, on the Bridge Street side of the crossing in central Cambridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole bridge, the water and the punts. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are standing close and the bridge will not fit. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the railings and the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Quayside (riverside on the quay, looking back at the bridge from the water's edge). The iron bridge spanning the river, with punts moored or drifting in the foreground beneath it and the riverside buildings lining the quays. The bridge lies to the north-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the bridge arch near the middle of the frame, with the water filling the lower third. Keep the horizon level so the span does not look tilted. Let a punt sit in the foreground for scale. If the view is blocked, wait a little; boats keep moving. The bank opposite the Quayside, on Magdalene Street, gives a side-on view of the bridge as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the ironwork stays dark and detailed rather than washed out. Try a Live Photo to catch punts gliding past, and choose the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to the water and ironwork. Early in the day there are usually fewer punts in the way.

text.access_note: The bridge and street are a public road and crossing, and the Quayside is a riverside street; check the official site before you go if you plan to visit any of the nearby colleges.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is generally kinder to water and ironwork than harsh midday sun.
There are usually fewer punts on the river early in the day than later on.
The bridge and street are open to the public as a normal road and crossing, with no entry restriction.

name: King's College Chapel
label: King's College Chapel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Backs' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Backs' (relation/1999158): edge nearest the subject (809 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/164848633: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'King's College Chapel' (104 m across).
notes: Gothic masterpiece with the famous fan-vaulted ceiling.

text.description: King's College Chapel is the great Gothic chapel of King's College and the building most people picture when they think of Cambridge. It was built in phases by a succession of English kings between the mid-1400s and 1515, and it holds the world's largest fan vault, finished in 1515 by master mason John Wastell. The tall windows and long, pale stone sides make it an easy subject for a phone, and the best-known view is across the water meadow rather than from the street. From The Backs, the far bank of the Cam, the chapel's west end rises above the lawn and willows, with the river and punts in the foreground. Guides call this the classic postcard view. The chapel is still an active place of worship and the home of the King's College Choir, so treat it as a working building rather than a film set. The long, flat meadow gives you room to choose your frame: a wide view with the willows and river, or a tighter shot of the west end alone. If you can, come early, when the footpaths are quiet. A second view, from King's Parade, shows the façade head-on from the street, which suits a straight, symmetrical shot.
text.geographic_location: In the historic centre of Cambridge, on the east side of the River Cam, with King's Parade on its street side and the Backs lawns running down to the river on the other. Clare College's buildings appear on the left in the view from Clare Bridge.
text.directions_text: Start from King's Parade in the centre of Cambridge, which is the easiest place to find the chapel from. Follow the river and the Back Lawn route and keep the chapel on your east side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic view with the lawn, willows and river. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the west end and its pinnacles. The ultra-wide (0.5x) works for a low shot with punts or willow branches close in the foreground, but the chapel will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in The Backs (far bank of the Cam, across the meadow from the Back Lawn). The chapel's west end rising above the lawn and willows, with the river and punts in the foreground. From there the chapel is to the east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the river or lawn in the lower third, with the chapel's west end above it. Keep the phone level so the tall verticals do not lean. For a different view, try Clare Bridge, which frames the chapel's west end beyond the bridge with Clare College's buildings on the left. King's Parade gives a head-on shot of the façade from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the chapel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the stone keeps its detail. Live Photos can catch punts drifting past, and panorama can take in the whole stretch of lawn if you hold the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, before the crowds arrive, when the footpaths are empty.

text.access_note: The college buildings are private and the chapel is an active place of worship, but the grounds and the Back Lawn route to the river can be photographed from outside. Check the official site before you go, as access can change.
claims_not_in_sources: The Backs are the lawns and meadows along the river behind the colleges.
The chapel is on the east side of the River Cam, with King's Parade on its street side.
Keeping the phone level helps stop tall buildings from appearing to lean.
Punts are likely to pass through the view during the day.

name: Trinity College
label: Trinity College
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Trinity Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Trinity Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/151180819: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Trinity College (University of Cambridge)' (514 m across).
notes: Largest college, with Great Court and the clock tower.

text.description: Trinity College is one of the biggest colleges in the University of Cambridge, and its front on Trinity Street is the part most visitors photograph. The Great Gate faces east, with a statue of Henry VIII above the archway. Henry founded the college in 1546 by merging two older colleges, Michaelhouse and King's Hall. Behind the gate is Great Court, said to be the largest enclosed courtyard in Europe. Further back, towards the river Cam, are Nevile's Court and the Wren Library. Most of the major buildings date from the 16th and 17th centuries. The gate works well for a phone because it is a single, strong subject with clear stonework and a statue to pick out. Stand on the cobbles outside it and you can show the whole frontage, or zoom in on the statue and archway. Early morning is best: the frontage is lit by the sun and the crowds have not built up. Delivery vans sometimes block the cobbles, so be ready to shift a few steps and wait for a clear moment. If you have time, Trinity Bridge over the Cam is a second option, with the college grounds and trees behind it. The grounds are private, so that view takes more planning than the gate.
text.geographic_location: Trinity College is in the centre of Cambridge. Its Great Gate opens onto Trinity Street, and the college grounds run back west towards the river Cam. St John's College is its neighbour.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Trinity Street in central Cambridge. Walk to the Great Gate on foot for the last stretch. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole Great Gate frontage. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to fit it all in. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the statue of Henry VIII above the archway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Trinity Street (in front of the Great Gate, on the cobbles outside the gate). The east-facing Great Gate frontage with Henry VIII's statue above the archway, best lit in the morning.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the gate up square-on, so the vertical edges of the stonework stay straight. Keep the phone level rather than tilting it up, and step back a little if you can. Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then a closer one of the statue and archway. If you want a second view, Trinity Bridge over the Cam shows the grounds and trees behind it. Confirm the exact spot to stand when you get there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out the top of the gate. Portrait mode is not needed here, but take a few frames in case a van or passer-by spoils one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the frontage is sunlit and the crowds have not formed.

text.access_note: The college grounds are privately owned.
claims_not_in_sources: Trinity Street is fairly narrow, so the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) may help fit the whole frontage in.
Tilting the phone upwards makes vertical lines lean inwards, so keeping it level helps keep the gate straight.
The sky behind the gate can be bright enough to need a lower exposure setting.

name: St John's College
label: St John's College
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kitchen Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Kitchen Bridge' (way/570077179): middle (22 m across); moved 10 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/151180816: large area 'St John's College (University of Cambridge)' (638 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Gatehouse and New Court, known as the wedding cake.

text.description:
St John's College is one of the largest colleges of the University of Cambridge. It was founded by Lady Margaret Beaufort, and its charter is dated 9 April 1511. The site beside the River Cam was once a medieval hospital, and over the following centuries the college grew westward towards the water. Today it has eleven courts, a chapel designed by George Gilbert Scott (the third tallest building in Cambridge) and the Bridge of Sighs. The Bridge of Sighs is the best-known feature seen from here.

Looking back at the college from upstream, you see the Bridge of Sighs arching over the Cam beside the New Court buildings. The river and the punts give the picture a natural frame and plenty of depth. Everything in the scene is close together, so it suits a phone well. You can take it in at the default lens (1x) and still have stonework, water and boats in one shot.

If Kitchen Bridge is busy, The Backs is a good alternative. It is a public footpath, and from the bank you can zoom in on the Bridge of Sighs with willows and punts in front. Garret Hostel Bridge also gives a river view with St John's behind and Trinity College on the other side of the frame. The Bridge of Sighs itself can only be crossed with a college ticket, so most people photograph it from outside.
text.geographic_location: St John's College stands beside the River Cam in central Cambridge, next to Trinity College. Its river frontage is part of the stretch known as The Backs.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so start in the centre of Cambridge and walk to St John's College. Head for the river side of the college, where Kitchen Bridge crosses the Cam upstream of the Bridge of Sighs. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of bridge, buildings, river and punts. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Bridge of Sighs and its stonework. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and water, and keep the bridge away from the edges of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kitchen Bridge (upstream of the Bridge of Sighs, looking back at the college). The Bridge of Sighs arching over the Cam beside the New Court buildings, framed by the river and punts.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the Bridge of Sighs on one of the third-lines, with the river running into the picture below it. Wait for a punt to drift into the lower part of the frame so the water has something to lead the eye. If the bridge is crowded, try The Backs for a zoomed-in view across the river, or Garret Hostel Bridge for a wider river view with St John's behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Take a few frames, as punts and the water keep moving. Live Photos can help you pick the best moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually quieter on the bridge and the river, and gentler light suits the stonework. Bright midday sun can leave the buildings and the water looking flat or glary.

text.access_note: Kitchen Bridge is on college land and the Bridge of Sighs can only be crossed with a college ticket, so check the official site before you go for opening times and any photography limits, especially in the chapel; The Backs is a public footpath.

name: Queens' College
label: Queens' College
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Silver Street Bridge' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Silver Street' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/148215569: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Queens' College (University of Cambridge)' (351 m across).
notes: Medieval college with timbered cloisters.

text.description: Queens' College is one of Cambridge's oldest colleges, founded in 1448 by Margaret of Anjou and refounded in 1465 by Elizabeth Woodville. That double start is why the name has the apostrophe after the s. The college is one of only two whose main buildings straddle the River Cam, and the two halves are joined by the wooden Mathematical Bridge. The photo most visitors come for is that bridge arching over the water, with the college's old brick courts rising behind it. Often a punt slides underneath, which gives the picture a little life. The Old Court is described as one of the best-preserved medieval groups of buildings in the city, and the President's Lodge, from around 1460, is the oldest building on the river here. The bridge itself is reserved for college members, so visitors photograph it from outside rather than walking across. Silver Street Bridge is a free public bridge, and it lets you frame the whole arch from above without going into the college. For a quieter angle, try Queens' Road, which looks across the river to the same bridge from beside the Backs. Take a few frames in portrait and a few in landscape. The curve of the arch, the water and the brick all work well in either, and the reflections are worth including if the water is calm.
text.geographic_location: Queens' College is in the south of central Cambridge, on both banks of the River Cam, mostly on the east bank. It sits right beside Silver Street and the Mathematical Bridge.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Cambridge, head south towards Silver Street. Silver Street Bridge is a public bridge near the Mathematical Bridge, so check the map for its exact position. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole arch of the Mathematical Bridge and the brick buildings behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the bridge parapet or other people crowd you in. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out the bridge and the old brick courts without moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Silver Street Bridge. The wooden Mathematical Bridge arching over the River Cam with the college's old brick courts behind it, often with a punt passing underneath. Check the map before choosing which side of the bridge to stand on.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the arch along the lower third, leaving room for the brick courts above it. Wait for a punt to drift under the bridge before you press the shutter. If you want a calmer picture with fewer people in it, walk to Queens' Road and shoot across the river from there instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wooden bridge to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the brick and timber keep their colour. A Live Photo can catch a punt moving through the frame, and you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is often calmer on the bridge, and softer daylight suits the brickwork. Any time works if you are patient for a punt to pass.

text.access_note: Silver Street Bridge is a free public bridge, but the college itself may charge for entry and the Mathematical Bridge is reserved for college members, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Earlier in the day is often calmer on the bridge than later.
Softer daylight tends to suit brickwork photos.
Reflections in calm water can add to the picture.
Phone lens suggestions (0.5x, 1x, 2x or more) are general phone advice, not specific to this view.
